html:
The New Hebrides was the colonial name for the island group in the South Pacific that is now Vanuatu. James Cook named it in 1774 after the Hebrides of Scotland. From 1906 to 1980 Britain and France ruled it jointly as a condominium. The map shows it in 1938.

The arrangement was unusual. Each power ran its own system, so there were two police forces, two sets of laws, two currencies and two school systems, with a joint court for land and shared matters. Settlers chose which law to live under, and islanders had no citizenship of either. People joked that the condominium was a "pandemonium".

Before that, from the 1860s, many ni-Vanuatu men had been recruited, often by deceit or force, to work on plantations in Queensland and Fiji, the trade called blackbirding. Presbyterian and Catholic missions spread through the islands, and coconut plantations produced copra.

In the late 1930s and early 1940s the John Frum movement arose on the island of Tanna. During the Second World War the island of Espiritu Santo became a large American base. The islands won independence as Vanuatu in 1980.
